$W_F$ ranges in $[0, 1]$ [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states in the notes and passages that $W_F$ (visibility-weighted saliency of feature F) is defined as the ratio of the sum of saliency values for voxels in feature F to the sum of saliency values for all voxels in the volume V. Since saliency values ($s_i$) are non-negative, this ratio inherently ranges from 0 (if feature F has no saliency) to 1 (if feature F contains all the saliency of the volume). The notes specifically mention 'ranging in [0, 1]' in the definition of $W_F$.

The source text explicitly defines 'visibility-weighted saliency' as a combination of 'feature visibility' (which measures contribution to the final image and accounts for occlusion/alpha blending) and 'saliency field' (which measures visual saliency/conspicuity relative to the local neighborhood using a center-surround operator, representing local distinctiveness). The text further states that this technique provides 'quantitative information' and allows features to be 'measured in a quantitative and fully automated way.' Therefore, every fact in the claim is supported by the evidence.

Perform front-to-back compositing along rays from the viewpoint [S2].

The claim states that front-to-back compositing is performed along rays from the viewpoint. Source [S2] explicitly defines the Visibility Field calculation using the formula 'vi = (1 - Ai-1) * ai', which is the standard mathematical definition of front-to-back compositing. Furthermore, the text describes the visibility field as indicating 'viewpoint-dependent occlusions' and being affected by 'voxels in front of the current voxel in the view direction.' Although the text also mentions a 'slice-based rendering' implementation detail for computational efficiency, the fundamental definition and the method described in the notes (and the core definition in the passage) rely on the front-to-back accumulation logic along the view direction (rays).

Unlike [Feature Visibility](6229-binary-and-soft-classification.md) which only measures occlusion/contribution, VWS also measures conspicuity (standing out from surroundings) via a center-surround operator on appearance attributes [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that unlike Feature Visibility (which measures occlusion/contribution), VWS (Visibility-Weighted Saliency) also measures conspicuity via a center-surround operator on appearance attributes. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in the notes and passages: 'Unlike feature visibility which only measures occlusion/contribution, visibility-weighted saliency also measures conspicuity (standing out from surroundings) via the center-surround operator on appearance attributes.' It further defines the saliency field $L(O, i, σ)$ using a center-surround operator on appearance attributes $O$ (such as brightness and saturation) and defines visibility-weighted saliency as the product of visibility (contribution) and saliency (conspicuity).
